source: Parsons and Shukla (2025) Beyond Problem Solving: Framing and Problem-Solution Co-Evolution in Data Visualization Design
finding: Expert visualization designers kept reframing the problem after solution attempts. Framing was a continuous activity, not a first step. Bridges between problem and solution were metaphors, heuristics, sketches, primary generators and reflection on failed ideas. Human study, not an LLM study.
numbers: N=11 expert practitioners; design challenge plus diaries plus one interview each; interviews 72 to 101 min, mean 87 min; reflexive thematic analysis (qualitative, no effect sizes).
quote: framing is not a preliminary step, but a continuous activity embedded in the act of designing
limits: Small self-selected expert sample, self-reported diaries, one domain, no machine arm.
agent_relevance: Supports a S2-S3 loop where a failed solution attempt triggers problem restatement. Names concrete reframing triggers (tool feedback, failed ideas) that code could detect.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero and Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing. CHI 25
finding: Large randomized test of three ways to use GPT-4o for problem reframing. None raised the novelty or usefulness of the problem frames over working alone.
numbers: N=280 analysed (456 recruited), 3 design problems, 4 arms: manual, direct, structured (Dorst nine-step chain), free-form. Frames rated for novelty and usefulness by 15 expert designers. All manual-vs-LLM and between-arm tests p>0.05 (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis). Sample sized for 95% power at a medium effect.
quote: using LLMs does not help improve the quality of problem frames
limits: Crowdsourced designers, one model (GPT-4o, Aug 2024, before o1 models), three problems, one-shot frames, no solution phase, so co-evolution itself was not tested. Absence of a significant difference is not proof of no effect.
agent_relevance: Strong null for a frame-generation step done by a model and handed to a person. Do not assume a reframe prompt improves frames; it needs a measured check.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero and Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing. CHI 25
finding: The structured arm followed Dorst's nine-step reframing process as a prompt chain. It cost more time and gave no quality gain.
numbers: Mean time for two frames: manual 23.25 min (SD 14.73), direct 21.82 (11.95), structured 28.35 (18.00), free-form 20.78 (9.34). Structured is about 22% slower than manual. Nearly all structured users regenerated all content at least once; most re-runs hit the apparent-problem step (n=39) and stakeholder step (n=25).
limits: Time is self-paced on a crowd platform. Chain was an adaptation of Dorst's process, run on one model.
agent_relevance: A longer scripted reframe chain is not a free upgrade. Keep any reframing step short, gated, and tested against a no-reframe arm at equal tokens.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero and Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing. CHI 25
finding: People felt helped by the LLM in every arm, yet quality did not move. Felt help is not evidence of better frames.
numbers: Creativity Support Index: direct 64.28 (SD 18.90), structured 64.85 (20.00), free-form 61.01 (17.19); all in the good-support band, no significant differences. NASA-TLX effort did not differ. Agency and ownership did not drop with LLM use (all p>0.05).
limits: Self-report scales. The index is not defined for the manual arm, so it has no manual comparison.
agent_relevance: Our agent should not use its own confidence or a user's satisfaction as a signal that a reframe worked. Use a code-checkable outcome.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero and Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing. CHI 25
finding: LLM help widened the gap between people who knew reframing and people who did not. Skilled users got more novel frames.
numbers: In LLM arms, experts produced 12.54% more novel frames than novices (z=2.70, p=0.01). Gap was largest in free-form at 20.84% (z=2.31, p=0.06, not significant). Experts felt 15.69% more agency in the structured arm (z=2.29, p=0.02). Usefulness gaps: none significant. Expert/novice split: 3 or more of 5 quiz items correct.
limits: Expertise was a short quiz, not practice. Subgroup analysis with several tests and modest p-values.
agent_relevance: The value of a reframe step may depend on the reader's ability to judge it. An agent with a weak judge may gain nothing from extra frames.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero and Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing. CHI 25
finding: Participants said why the LLM frames did not help: not new, repetitive, not useful. Some said the AI did the thinking for them.
numbers: 93 of 218 LLM-arm users reported trouble building on LLM frames: not novel n=31, repetitive n=14, not useful n=12. Authors say 34% of respondents named non-novel frames as the obstacle.
quote: I didn't have to think very hard since the AI did everything
limits: Open-text answers, coded by the authors.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema's null result on LLM reframing. Frames from one model tend to look alike, so a reframe operator needs a diversity control, not just a prompt.

source: Sood, Wan, Paris and Grace (2026) What makes LLM-generated Answers Valuable for Research Problem Reframing? ICCC26 paper 78
finding: Small study where researchers judged LLM answers to their own research questions. A four-call chain based on Dorst's first steps was liked more than a plain prompt or a prompt with all notes.
numbers: N=7 research students; 27 answers each (3 questions x 3 strategies x 3 answers) from GPT-oss-120b. Marked interesting: dorst-frame 29 of 189, direct 17 of 189, all-content 17 of 189. Top-3 per person (21 answers): dorst-frame 11 (52%), direct 7 (33%), all-content 3 (14%). Six of 7 liked dorst-frame most in the first pass; 4 of 7 in the top-3 ranking.
limits: N=7, convenient sample, outcome is interest, not correctness or improvement. Answers for one question-strategy were told to differ from earlier ones, so they are not independent. No no-LLM arm, no solution phase.
agent_relevance: Weak positive for a structured problem-side chain, in tension with Shin et al. Interest is cheap to get; verified improvement is not shown.

source: Sood, Wan, Paris and Grace (2026) What makes LLM-generated Answers Valuable for Research Problem Reframing? ICCC26 paper 78
finding: Two kinds of useful answer: those that confirm the user's thinking, and those that change it. Different survey items track each.
numbers: Seven 7-point items on top-3 answers (21 answers). Cluster 1 (Q1 taught me something, Q3 challenges my thinking, Q4 connects to something new) = reorienting. Cluster 2 (Q2 cleared my thinking, Q5 on the right track) = reinforcing. Five of 7 participants said top answers made them rethink their question.
limits: N=7; clusters from 21 ratings by Spearman correlation; self-report.
agent_relevance: Gives a usable split for an agent: tag a reframe as reinforcing (keeps the frame) or reorienting (replaces it), and only count the second as a reframe.

source: Sood, Wan, Paris and Grace (2026) What makes LLM-generated Answers Valuable for Research Problem Reframing? ICCC26 paper 78
finding: What made answers useless: wrong terms, invented assumptions, no support, ignoring the question, forced links between papers.
numbers: Examples from participants P1 to P7; theory-heavy notes (P7) gave the worst results because the model forced connections. The dorst-frame strategy uses 4 sequential calls (Archaeology, Paradox, Context, Frames), each fed the previous output plus full notes.
limits: Qualitative. Only steps 1-3 and 6 of Dorst's nine steps were used.
agent_relevance: Failure types are checkable in an agent: unsupported assumption, unanswered question, forced link. These can be audit items for a reframe.

source: Sood, Wan, Paris and Grace (2026) What makes LLM-generated Answers Valuable for Research Problem Reframing? ICCC26 paper 78
finding: Dorst's own frame method is problem-first. Its first three steps deepen understanding of the problem before any frame appears. Using it in an LLM chain is therefore not a test of co-evolution.
numbers: Nine steps: archaeology, paradox, context, field, themes, frames, futures, transformation, integration. The authors state steps 1 to 3 come before any frame is proposed.
limits: Reading of the paper's own description; no experiment on order.
agent_relevance: For the open question of problem-first versus co-evolve, neither Shin nor Sood compares orders. This stays untested for LLMs.

source: Zhang, Gu, Chen, Ding, Chai and Fan (year not stated on page) Leveraging LLMs to emulate the design processes of different cognitive styles. AHFE
finding: Zero-shot chain-of-thought prompts were written to make an LLM act as a problem-driven or a solution-driven designer (Dorst and Cross 2001). Static features matched humans. The back-and-forth between problem and solution did not.
numbers: Abstract page only. No figures on the page. Reported: static distribution of cognitive issues matched human data from prior studies; solution novelty and integrity above baseline prompts; problem-solution transitions less complex than human designers.
quote: LLMs lack the fully complex nonlinear transitions between problem and solution spaces observed in human designers
limits: Abstract only; model not named; numbers not seen; full text not opened. Treat details as unverified.
agent_relevance: Hint that a model can write problem and solution steps but does not move between them as people do. Our loop must force the return move.

source: Microsoft Research (2026) Theory Under Construction: Orchestrating Language Models for Research Software Where the Specification Evolves (Comet-H), arXiv 2604.27209
finding: An LLM agent loop where the goal, theory, code and claims are allowed to change together. The prompt controller picks the next prompt by what the workspace lacks. One tool built this way beat the next baseline by a wide margin.
numbers: Tool a3 (Python static analysis) F1=0.768 on a 90-case benchmark; next-best baseline 0.364. Portfolio: 46 repositories, 12+ domains, about 400 commits. Controller is a hand-weighted linear scorer over prompt families (a contextual bandit).
limits: Authors' own benchmark and portfolio, one in-depth case, no human or no-loop control arm at equal compute. The controller ablations in Table 7 are predicted signatures; I did not see a measured table for them.
agent_relevance: Closest working example of an agent loop where the problem (spec) changes with the solution. Shows the idea is practical, not that it beats a fixed spec.

source: Microsoft Research (2026) Theory Under Construction: Orchestrating Language Models for Research Software Where the Specification Evolves (Comet-H), arXiv 2604.27209
finding: In this loop the model first grew the project outward, then contracted it. Late commits were mostly audits. The model retracted claims that failed and picked a new angle.
numbers: Observation 1: audit and contraction dominate late phases of successful runs (about 400 commits, descriptive). a3 moved from generic analyzer to precision-focused bug filter. Another repo reports 85.7% repair on a controlled benchmark and 9.1% failure out of distribution.
limits: Authors state these are descriptive patterns from git history, not causal claims. No counts for how often each move occurred.
agent_relevance: Supports a reframe-then-contract pattern: let scope drift, then force a grounding and audit pass. Forced grounding stopped the model from just adding features.

source: Microsoft Research (2026) Theory Under Construction: Orchestrating Language Models for Research Software Where the Specification Evolves (Comet-H), arXiv 2604.27209
finding: Design choices that kept a long co-evolving loop bounded: unfinished follow-ups fade with a half-life, claims are re-checked against code whenever docs change, and a ledger tracks audited claims.
numbers: Components named: grounding ledger, half-life on carried follow-ups, adjacency scoring of prompts against workspace deficits, paper-first skeleton. Table 7 lists what each removal is predicted to cause (for example: no ledger gives a larger unsupported-claim surface).
limits: Predicted, not measured, for the controller ablations I saw. Single research group.
agent_relevance: Gives concrete, code-checkable pieces to copy: a ledger of claims, decay on open items, re-check on change.

source: Huang et al. (2026) R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data. ICLR 2026
finding: A model split into a question-writer (Challenger) and a solver. The Challenger is rewarded for questions at the edge of the Solver's ability. Both improved over three rounds with no human data. This is task and solver co-evolution, not frame and solution co-evolution.
numbers: Qwen3-8B-Base math average 49.18 to 54.69 (+5.51) after 3 iterations. OctoThinker-3B 26.64 to 29.32 (+2.68). Qwen3-4B-Base +6.49 on math and +7.54 on general reasoning.
limits: Training method (GRPO), not a scaffold. Math-focused data. Majority-vote pseudo-labels.
agent_relevance: Adapting what question is asked to current solver ability is a real lever. For a scaffold-only agent it maps to choosing the next subproblem by difficulty.

source: Huang et al. (2026) R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data. ICLR 2026
finding: The co-evolving loop degraded its own labels as questions got harder. A filter on answer consistency was needed.
numbers: Pseudo-label accuracy fell from 79.0% to 63.0% by iteration 3. Solver accuracy on Challenger questions fell to 47.0% by step 45. Removing task filtering cut the general-domain average by over 6 points.
limits: Label accuracy measured on a 200-question sample, labelled by a stronger model.
agent_relevance: A self-set problem drifts toward ill-posed items unless a consistency filter and an outside check hold it. Matches our guardrails against self-agreement.

source: Huang et al. (2026) R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data. ICLR 2026
finding: Boundary: the loop helps larger models for longer. Small models turn down early.
numbers: Smaller models start to decline after about step 15; the largest (4B) sustained gains longer. The 0.6B model begins to decline while label accuracy is still 70.6%.
limits: Step counts read from text and Table 7; one model family (Qwen3).
agent_relevance: If the agent's base model is weak, a self-driven reframe loop may hurt. Gate loop depth by model strength.

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks? NeurIPS 2025 D&B
finding: Models can solve a problem once it is complete, but often fail to ask the one question that completes it. This is the solution-to-problem return move in its simplest form.
numbers: Four domains: Logic-Q, Planning-Q, GSM-Q, GSME-Q (at most one missing variable; pick the right clarifying question from choices). Best models are above 80% on GSM-Q and GSME-Q but at most about 50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q. Tested zero-shot, chain-of-thought and four-shot.
quote: struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Multiple-choice format; single missing variable only; model-by-condition cells in my PDF text were scrambled, so I quote headline ranges only.
agent_relevance: An agent that can only solve, not ask, will sit in S3 without returning to S2. Add an explicit what-is-missing check, and do not assume it is easy.

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks? NeurIPS 2025 D&B
finding: How hard the what-is-missing step is depends on search depth in the logic domain, but not in planning. Math is easy for a different reason.
numbers: On the full sets GPT-4o reaches 99.39% on GSME-Q and 84.05% on GSM-Q. In Logic-Q, accuracy correlates negatively with search difficulty (about -0.1 to -0.24 across models); in Planning-Q the correlation is weak or none. Verbalised math (GSM-Q) was harder than equation form (GSME-Q).
limits: Correlations are per-model and small; dataset built from synthetic constraint problems.
agent_relevance: The missing-information step is not one skill. Do not expect one prompt to fix it across logic, planning and word problems.

source: Mu et al. (2024) ClarifyGPT: Empowering LLM-based Code Generation with Intention Clarification. FSE 2024
finding: A pipeline that detects an unclear requirement, asks clarifying questions, then writes code raised GPT-4 accuracy in a human-in-the-loop test.
numbers: Ten participants, 140 ambiguous MBPP-sanitized problems, 2.85 questions per problem, three answerers per problem. GPT-4 Pass@1 on MBPP-sanitized 70.96% to 80.80% (relative +13.87%); MBPP-ET after-value 60.19% (relative +16.83%); average 70.50%. Best baselines (CoT, GPT-Engineer) about 9.5 points lower.
limits: Small human study. Text and table disagree on which model the MBPP-ET baseline 51.52% belongs to, so I quote after-values. Ambiguity detection uses code consistency on generated tests.
agent_relevance: Real data that returning to the problem (clarify) beats solving straight away on ambiguous coding tasks. Detection by checking agreement of sampled programs is a code-checkable trigger.

source: Mu et al. (2024) ClarifyGPT: Empowering LLM-based Code Generation with Intention Clarification. FSE 2024
finding: Same pipeline with a simulated user over four benchmarks: gains of about 10 to 13 points for GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-4 Pass@1 gains: HumanEval +11.34, HumanEval-ET +10.35, MBPP-sanitized +10.89, MBPP-ET +13.49; four-benchmark average 68.02% to 75.75%. The FSE version reports different averages, so treat averages as version-dependent.
limits: Simulated answers come from a model that may see ground truth, which can overstate gains. Needs instruction-tuned models.
agent_relevance: Supports adding a gated clarify step. The gate (only when ambiguous) matters: do not ask when the task is clear.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: Model picks, adapts and fills a task-level reasoning plan once, then follows it per instance. A one-shot frame, not a loop with the solution.
numbers: PaLM 2-L: BBH 56% to 67% (CoT 60%), T4D 30% to 69% (CoT 40%), MATH 45% to 50.5%. GPT-4: BBH 58% to 81% (CoT 75%), T4D 51% to 85%, MATH 70.5% to 73%. Beats CoT on 21 of 25 tasks; 10 to 40 times less inference compute than some multi-sample methods.
limits: Adjacent, not a co-evolution test: frame chosen before solving, never revised after failure. 74.7% of MATH failures were computation errors, which a frame cannot fix.
agent_relevance: A cheap frame-first step has measured value on some tasks. A fair test of co-evolution would add a revise-frame-after-failure arm to this baseline.

source: Ege et al. (2024) ChatGPT as an inventor: eliciting the strengths and weaknesses of current LLMs against humans in engineering design (arXiv 2404.18479)
finding: In a 48-hour prototyping hackathon an LLM led two human hands. It had strong concepts but dropped promising ideas on small snags, added needless complexity and fixated.
numbers: ChatGPT 4.0 placed second of six teams; more than 100 prototypes in the data set; six recommendations including prompting for alternatives and iterative feedback loops.
limits: Abstract-page level only here; no counts for how often each behavior occurred. One hackathon, one model. Fuller detail is in b17.
agent_relevance: Shows the opposite risk to over-persisting: abandoning a frame at the first sign of trouble. A reframe trigger needs a threshold.

source: Sygkounas et al. (2026) COvolve: adversarial co-evolution of LLM-generated policies and environments (arXiv 2603.28386; GECCO 2026)
finding: LLMs write both the test environments and the policies as code and play a zero-sum game. A mixed Nash policy keeps old skills. Another task-solver co-evolution, not frame-solution.
numbers: Abstract page only: urban driving, symbolic maze, geometric navigation; reports progressively more complex environments. No numbers seen.
limits: No figures read; full PDF text could not be extracted (file was damaged on download).
agent_relevance: Low relevance. Listed so it is not mistaken for evidence on design co-evolution.

source: Gap note for this pass (Angle C)
finding: Search found no LLM study that tests problem-first against co-evolving order, or codes LLM design protocols for problem-solution transitions with numbers. Only one qualitative claim (AHFE) says LLMs lack the nonlinear moves.
numbers: Searches run: LLM + co-evolution + design; solution-jumping; requirements clarification; reframing; self-evolving. Human-AI co-evolution studies by Guo et al. and Chen et al. are in evidence_b.jsonl (b08, b09, b10) and not repeated here. O'Hara (2025) on solution-jumping is a24 in evidence_a.jsonl.
limits: A negative search result, not proof. Several relevant items (ICCC26, DRS2026) are very recent and thinly indexed.
agent_relevance: The schema's S2-S3 loop has no direct LLM trial in the literature found. Our own equal-token test (SUBFIELDS item 2) would be new evidence.

source: Cross-study comparison: Shin et al. (2025) versus Sood et al. (2026)
finding: The two reframing studies seem to disagree but they measure different things. Shin: rated novelty and usefulness by experts, N=280, null. Sood: the user's own interest, N=7, favours the structured chain.
numbers: Shin: 4 arms, no difference (p>0.05). Sood: 29 vs 17 vs 17 interesting out of 189 each; 11 of 21 top-3.
limits: Different models (GPT-4o vs GPT-oss-120b), tasks (product design problems vs own research questions), judges (15 raters vs the author of the question).
agent_relevance: Interest in an answer should not be treated as quality. For the agent, a reframe is judged by what it changes in a checkable outcome.

source: Secondary reports on ClarifyCoder and ClarifyCodeBench (search summaries only)
finding: Follow-on work reports that clarification-aware fine-tuning raised how often the model asks and asks well, and that ambiguity cuts coding accuracy.
numbers: ClarifyCoder: communication rate +40 and good-question rate +30 points absolute (search summary). ClarifyCodeBench via a blog: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Pass@1 48.8% to 38.2% under ambiguity (unverified).
limits: Not opened; figures come from search snippets and a third-party blog; do not cite without checking the originals.
agent_relevance: Pointer for a later pass.

source: Joint read of Shin et al. (2025) and Sood et al. (2026): what is missing
finding: Both studies stop after the frame. Neither lets the model try a solution and then revise the frame, which is the core of co-evolution.
numbers: Shin: frames submitted, no solution step. Sood: answers ranked, no solution step. Comet-H (c12) and ClarifyGPT (c20) do loop back, but they test spec change and clarification rather than design frames.
limits: Reading across papers, not new data.
agent_relevance: An LLM test of co-evolution needs three arms at equal tokens: frame-first, solve-first with revise, and loop. None exists in what I found.
